catalog_quote: 1. Stress Stress occurs on the last syllable of the word. It is manifested by having more emphasis, loudness, etc. In the following words, stress is on the last syllable: qá'áb 'sack', seqí 'my feet', guli 'skunk', dadáben 'medicine', selatax 'palm of my hand'. 2. Tone contrasts and allotones In Chilcotin there is a contrast of three tones: high versus low versus a downgliding contour. In words of two syllables there are the following patterns: low-low, low-high, high-low, high-high, high-contour and low-contour.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Chilcotin is a tone language (high vs low vs word-final downgliding contour, with progressive tone sandhi); independently of tone, word stress (greater emphasis/loudness) falls on the last syllable of every word, i.e. fixed final stress. The examples include words whose stressed final syllable carries low tone (guli, selatax) as well as high tone (seqí), so stress is not a reflex of high tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by Pike, Radney & King. Ham (2008: 25 fn. 19) marks primary and secondary stress in her phonetic transcriptions but gives no rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for stress. (Tone: many words do or do not trigger sandhi lexically; guyi 'that' keeps its contour tone.) Tone-mark readings in the quoted examples (qá'áb, seqí, dadában) are transcribed from a typescript scan and should be checked against the page scan.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms elicited from three speakers of the Alexis Creek area (footnote 1); tone sandhi described at phrase level. Segmental phonemes follow Cook 1983; spelling in the practical orthography. Note that Krauss 1975 §1.4 and Cook 2013 Introduction describe only tone and say nothing about stress; Cook 2013 ch. 1 (unseen) has no stress section in its table of contents.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Chilcotin (Tsilhqot'in, ISO clc, glottocode chil1280) as spoken in the Alexis Creek area, British Columbia (footnote 1); Krauss 1975 §0.2 says the speech community is dialectally quite uniform. The Glottolog language-level name 'Chilcotin-Nicola' also covers extinct Nicola, which none of these sources describe.

tone_statements.citation: Rhyasen, Corrie. 1995. Chilcotin tone: an autosegmental analysis. Calgary Working Papers in Linguistics 17 (Winter 1995): 17-38. Calgary: Department of Linguistics, University of Calgary.
tone_statements.quote: Chilcotin appears to fall into the high-tone group of languages because its stems are lexically marked for high tone. If the stem is not marked for high tone then it is lexically toneless. There is no lexical low tone in Chilcotin. Toneless segments not associated with a high tone are marked for phonetic low tone by a default rule (Rice 1987, 1989). ... The first person duoplural prefix /id-/ always has a high tone. The presence of the /id-/ prefix causes alternations of the stem tone. In most cases /id-/ causes the stem tone to reverse; that is, if the stem has a high tone then affixation of /id-/ would reverse it to a low tone.

sources.note: Secondary autosegmental analysis of Chilcotin stem-tone alternations. Stems are lexically H or toneless (no lexical L; default L rule); the 1st-person duoplural prefix /id-/ carries H and triggers stem tone 'reversal' (L->H by H-spreading, H->L by OCP-driven deletion) and, sentence-finally, an H->HL falling pattern on a lengthened vowel which is argued not to be a true contour tone. No statement about stress.
